So there is a huge plea from the Ukrainians to the Americans to basically push SpaceX to allow them to have access to Starlink over Russian territory so that they can go after the launch sites from which these ballistic missiles are raining down on them.

Interestingly and alarmingly, something that I hadn't really focused on until I went to Ukraine and sort of really delved into this, the Russians have been and are building their own version of Starlink called Rassvet, which is still in its early stages. I think they put a couple of dozen or so satellites into space, nowhere near as many as Elon Musk has with SpaceX. But nonetheless, this capability is growing, and most people think that sometime in the next year or so, the Russians will have some Starlink equivalent, which will mean that they will be very easily able to direct and monitor drones going anywhere over Ukrainian territory, which will be another big blow to the Ukrainians.
DAVIES: And if the Ukrainians haven't had access to the Starlink system in Russian territory, how have they been able to manage these attacks on Russian facilities?

MINTON BEDDOES: I mean, there are other ways of guiding, but they're not as good as Starlink. The Ukrainians are incredibly innovative. And I think the important thing for people to understand is that thus far, Ukraine has sort of been ahead of the Russians in drone innovation, and they've been amazing at building up this drone industry. They've been always in a sort of cat-and-mouse game, somewhat ahead of the Russians. The Russians have been able to scale up. They're, you know, a bigger economy. They're good at scaling up their innovations. And what's slightly alarming now is it seems as though the Russians are actually ahead on innovation as well as an ability to scale.

I have no doubt that the Ukrainians will come up with new innovations, both in defensive drones and other areas. The question that is more uncertain right now is, do they have the financial capability and financial support to scale those innovations? And that's what really matters right now, because the truth is that Ukraine is very, very dependent on financial support. Unfortunately, there's no support coming from the U.S. anymore. When the Trump administration came in, the - until then, there had been a lot of support from the United States. Now there is really essentially none. Ukraine is financed by the Europeans, and the question is whether the Europeans will step up the pace of their financial support such that the Ukrainians have the money to scale up their drone program, which is essential to defend themselves.

DAVIES: Yeah. I want to talk more about that in a moment. But I also wanted to just note the level of Russian casualties in this war. It seems that the Ukrainians have been able to inflict terrible punishment on the Russian forces, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: The level of casualties are just extraordinary, something on the order of 40,000 people a month - Russians - killed and wounded. This is an unfathomable number of people. But one thing that's important to remember is we've been talking about all of the ways in which Russia is bombarding Ukraine. But Ukraine is, you know, essentially holding the front line and actually making a few gains in certain places.

So the sort of overall picture of this war is that the Ukrainians have held off the Russians. The front lines have been basically stable. The Russians, at incredible cost - 40,000 people a month - I mean, it just - you know, and you can't - it's hard to imagine those numbers. And they're still not able to really make a lot of progress. In some areas, they're gaining a tiny bit of ground. In some areas, they're losing. But basically the front lines are stable. So what the Russians have decided to do, particularly in recent weeks, knowing that they are not making serious progress at the front line, is to try and break the morale of Ukrainian civilians by completely bombarding the cities.

DAVIES: You know, there's a graph that you have in the article that came from your trip. It's a bar graph that shows, by year, how much money the Western allies have contributed to Ukraine's defense, and they're color-coded. You know, so much for the EU, so much for the United States, so much for other countries. And it was stunning to look - and I think it's in 2025 that the U.S. portion disappears. I'm not sure that much of the United States realizes that U.S. support for Ukraine has vanished completely.

MINTON BEDDOES: Yep. There is essentially no financial support for Ukraine from the United States. To the extent that there is any weaponry going, it is weaponry that is being bought by the Europeans on behalf of the Ukrainians from the U.S. When - you know, when President Trump came in, it became very clear that he did not intend to continue supporting Ukraine, and that has happened completely. And I don't think that's that well-known. And what is even less well-known is the degree to which the Europeans have stepped up and basically are single-handedly supporting Ukraine.

Now, this is because it's also, of course - it's our continent. It's in our own interest as Europeans to do that. But I am very clear, having just been there, that the situation is very, very stark right now and that I don't think the rest of the world has realized the degree that Russia is attacking civilians - there's no simpler way, no other way of putting it - attacking civilians and civilian life - and that, in order to be able to survive that and mount a defense, the Ukrainians need faster and more financial support so that they can scale up their defensive capability and so that they can survive. And this country has been extraordinarily resilient in the last 4 1/2 years. And yet it looks to me more difficult than it has for a long time in this war...
MINTON BEDDOES: ...Without financial support.

DAVIES: One of the issues is - is Zelenskyy still trusted as a leader? I mean, there have been some corruption cases. There are pieces of legislation in the legislature which have not been adopted. What's your sense of Zelenskyy's leadership and to what extent his credibility is undermining the kind of support either in the country or among allies?

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think there is growing frustration politically within Ukraine with President Zelenskyy and his leadership. I think that's - in some ways, that's kind of normal after 4 1/2 years of war. There is corruption in Ukraine, undoubtedly. The anti-corruption unit, which has been set up and is funded by the European Union as an important part of the prerequisites that Ukraine has to have to eventually become a member of the European Union - this organization is effective, is powerful, is unearthing corruption. There is corruption in the highest echelons of government around - or at least there are accusations of it in the highest echelons of government.

You know, this makes it more difficult. And as you say, Parliament - the Ukrainian Parliament has not passed some elements of some laws that the Europeans would like them to have passed as part of the sort of cleaning up of Ukraine. So that's very frustrating for the Europeans. It's not a perfect political situation.

On the other hand, this is a country fighting for its existence. And I'm not sure that this is as much a story of terrible corruption in Ukraine as it is a good-news story of the effectiveness of an anti-corruption unit shining a spotlight. And I see it as a sort of - a good sign that they're unearthing this and that they are, you know, shining the light on corruption where it is. And that's all part and parcel of Ukraine becoming more and more like the, you know, part of Europe that it should be.

But it's very difficult right now. You know, there should have been elections. Were it not for the war, there would have been elections. President Zelenskyy has been president a long time. In any country, he definitely is not someone who is so focused on institutional reform as he should be. There are huge shortcomings to elements of what President Zelenskyy does. But I wouldn't conclude from that that, you know, it's a terribly corrupt place, and therefore, we shouldn't support it. I think it's remarkable what the Ukrainians are doing, given what they're facing.

DAVIES: All right. We're going to take another break here. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. She'll be back to talk more after this short break. I'm Dave Davies, and this is FRESH AIR.

MINTON BEDDOES: Well, I actually think some oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz under the new arrangements that the U.S. military has put in place. MINTON BEDDOES: Both sides say that, you know, there is a deal to be done, but that deal is the one on their terms. I think it seems to me unlikely that there is going to be a serious resolution anytime soon because Iran is determined to have a resolution much more on its terms, which President Trump is not willing to have. And Iran - you know, the Iranian regime is showing that it has an incredible capacity to endure economic pain. And I think where we are now is we have a U.S. government that is convinced that the more it can tighten the economic screws on Iran, at some point, the Iranian regime is going to have to cave and come to a deal on U.S. terms. And we have an Iranian regime, which, of course, has several factions within it, of which at least the hard-liners are absolutely not - determined not to cave and have shown themselves willing to inflict incredible pain on their population.

So my sense is that the likely outcome is some version of the status quo for a while. And then either President Trump decides that he's going to go and try and bombard them into submission, or we go back to the agreement that was, you know, temporarily reached a few months ago, which is much more advantageous to Iran.

DAVIES: There was a story a while back that the Saudis had asked Trump to bomb the Houthis, who are making gains against the Saudi-backed regime in Yemen, and that Trump thought about doing it but in the end didn't. I mean, the problem, of course, is that when you increase hostilities in one place, there's a reaction elsewhere. You know, the Iranians can attack American allies. And Trump's kind of in a box here, isn't he?

MINTON BEDDOES: I actually think that that was a very meaningful moment. That decision, you're right. It appears that the Saudis asked for help, and, you know, President Trump decided no. If you stand back from this, we may well find that however this war turns out, it ends up being a turning point in the U.S. relationship with the region. And this was the story we put on our cover last week and looked into in some detail. And let me explain why I think that. You know, what have we learned from this war now? First of all, we've learned that the Gulf countries which relied on U.S. bases for their security have found that, actually, having U.S. bases doesn't necessarily provide you with security.
DAVIES: It can make you a target, right?

MINTON BEDDOES: It can make you a target. We found that there's been a huge use of U.S. munitions, which is going to have knock-on effects for U.S. security all around the world. And we've learned that probably going forward, you know, what U.S. bases remain in the region will have to be moved and probably put underground to be safe because we are now in this new drone-based warfare, which changes the calculus. If you add all of that together, it seems to me that it may well be that the sort of medium-term impact of this is fewer U.S. forces in different places and, thus, less of a U.S. footprint in the region. And instead, players from Iran, depending on what happens there, to Turkey, to, of course, Israel on the other side are going to be shaping the region sort of with less of an active U.S. involvement than there was. I think we may look back in a couple of decades and see this Iran war as being a turning point. I mean, I'm not suggesting the U.S. is going to leave completely, but I think the U.S. is going to be less involved than it was.

DAVIES: Let's talk about the state of U.S.-Western Europe alliances. You know, Trump condemned European countries that declined to support his war against Iran and help him with the blockade of Iran. MINTON BEDDOES: Well, there's just been a great agreement on Greenland - right? - where we've now got a formal agreement to the status quo effectively.
DAVIES: Right, kind of it gives the U.S. access to places that it pretty much had access to already access to before.

MINTON BEDDOES: Which it had access to before, exactly. Look, I think the big picture is that, first of all, the Europeans have woken up, not before time, to the need to build up their own defensive capability, to spend more on defense. And frankly, President Trump deserves a lot of credit for pushing the Europeans to do that, because for too long, the Europeans have been freeloading off the United States.

At the same time, however, there is a growing sense within Europe of, we're just not sure whether we can rely on the U.S. And, you know, Greenland was one example. MINTON BEDDOES: ...A kind of, you know, recognition. And I don't think - people haven't really worked out what to do. Within Europe, there are some Europeans who are still saying, eschew it (ph), absolutely. We can't do anything without the Americans. We must keep this alliance going. Then there are others - you know, the French in particular - who are pushing and always have in a sort of Gaullist way for a more European-only approach. And I'm not in the kind of business of pearl-clutching for what was. I think the challenge now for Europeans and for many others around the world is to, in a kind of eyes-wide-open way, say, OK. This is the United States we have now. It is the United States that has a different view of alliances than it used to. It's extraordinarily powerful. It's the country leading in the AI revolution that is going to shape warfare and our economies and everything else. What's our relationship with this country, and what are we going to do for ourselves? And that's the question we're beginning to ask ourselves in Europe. Unfortunately, we don't yet have a good answer.

DAVIES: Are Europeans looking towards the midterm elections to alter the course of American foreign policy at all, do you think?
MINTON BEDDOES: I think everyone around the world is transfixed by American politics, particularly right now.

MINTON BEDDOES: There is a - an expectation, a hope, that something will change after the midterms. I mean, the - they - you know, Europeans can look at the polling as well as anybody else. And you know that - I think according to our own forecast - we, as you know, have a midterm forecast model, which gives - I think it's, like, a 93% chance now that the House goes to the Democrats. And it's something like a 60% chance that the Senate does.
DAVIES: And I was surprised by that. Yeah.

MINTON BEDDOES: Yeah. There's a hope that that will happen. I have to say, my own expectation is that even if that happens, I don't expect an enormous change in American foreign policy. In fact, if anything, I worry that President Trump will focus more on foreign policy if the Democrats are in charge in Congress as a way of distracting attention. And there's an awful lot that the president can do, as you know, without Congress in the foreign policy arena.

DAVIES: Well, you know, Canada is an interesting case. I mean, you mentioned this. Mark Carney made that speech in Davos about middle powers having to seek an independent path and not rely on the alliances they have in the past. I mean, he's also said recently that he speaks frequently with President Trump and that they get along personally. I mean, what do you make of him, his course? And he's also talked about joining the EU as - what? - an associate member or something. And if - I don't even know if that's a thing.

MINTON BEDDOES: I actually think Mark Carney has done a really extraordinary job at managing a situation that is very, very difficult as Canadian prime minister. And I've known Prime Minister Carney for a while. He used to be a - you know, when he was governor of the Bank of England, and before that, he was a central banker in Canada. And I used to write about economics, so I've known him for a long time. And I am struck by how well this technocratic former central banker has become a very effective politician.

And his - as far as I can see, his strategy is one to really try and reshape the Canadian economy to make it more resilient - to, you know, cut regulation, to build up its defense, to make it a much more effective domestic economy. He also wants to try and build up trading relationships with others - you know, particularly Europe, but also, you remember he was in China not so long ago - so that he - over time, the Canadian economy becomes less reliant on the U.S. But I think he's also very well aware that at the moment, the Canadian economy is incredibly integrated with the U.S.

So there is this difficult balancing act between trying to work with President Trump, negotiate with President Trump, but also, politically, he can't cave to whatever, you know, crazy demands the American administration may make. And so I think it's very sensible to be talking a lot to President Trump and to try and have a working relationship. It's also important to stand up when something completely impossible is put on by the American side and to try and do the reforms that make your own economy as strong as possible and to try and build up relationships with others. It's a tough thing to do all of those things, but actually, I think he's been doing pretty well.

DAVIES: We need to take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Zanny Minton Beddoes. She is editor in chief for The Economist. We'll continue our conversation in just a moment. This is FRESH AIR.
(SOUNDBITE OF TODD SICKAFOOSE'S "BARNACLE")
DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. And our guest today is The Economist's editor in chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes. Our interview was recorded yesterday.

You know, there have been right-wing populist parties that have made significant gains in a number of European countries - France, you know, Germany, Italy, of course - Giorgia Meloni. I'm just wondering how you think that affects relations with the United States. Does Trump find friendly voices and support there that reinforce his own goals, do you think?

MINTON BEDDOES: So I think next year, 2027, is going to be a really pivotal year for Europe. There are elections in a number of European countries, but most importantly in France. And right now, as you know, Marine Le Pen leads the polls. I think there is a very real chance that Marine Le Pen, head of the RN - the populist-right party - could be the next president of France. And at the same time, the more extreme, right-wing AfD in Germany is not anywhere near power at the federal level, but is certainly the most successful party at the polls and winning at state-government level.

Europe could see populist right-wing governments in power in one or more countries next year. The question is, what does that mean for the whole European Union project? What does it mean for Europe's own decision-making? What does it mean for Europe's willingness to continue to support Ukraine? And what does it mean for Europe's relationship with the United States?

And I think it's an - there's sort of an interesting thing to watch here, 'cause on the one hand, you're right that some of these parties have had very close ties with MAGA, you know, have very strong ties with the Trump administration. But on the other hand, the more sort of bullying the Trump administration is towards Europe, the more difficult it is for a populist nationalist party to be too closely associated. So if you look - for example, Giorgia Meloni, the prime minister of Italy - she was very close to President Trump. But over time, she has had to distance herself because it's just very unpopular domestically.

So I think there are two separate questions. Will there be populist, nationalist governments in Europe next year, and what does it mean for Europe? And then separately, how will those governments behave towards the United States? And I don't think necessarily those two things point in the same direction.
DAVIES: And how do those populist parties regard Russia and its, you know, territorial ambitions in Ukraine?

MINTON BEDDOES: It's interesting. There's an interesting division between them. Giorgia Meloni has been very pro-Ukraine, very clearly, you know, with the European mainstream in supporting Ukraine. Interestingly, just in the last couple of weeks, Marine Le Pen and her party put out a statement loudly criticizing the Russian hybrid attacks in Europe and saying how unacceptable it was. The one party that is seen as being very pro-Russian, very determined to end support for Ukraine, is the German Alternative fur Deutschland - the German AfD. And that's the party that people are most worried about as being really, very close to the Russians.
DAVIES: Interesting. Over the summer, the United Kingdom got a new prime minister - Andy Burnham. What are some of the challenges he faces? Seventh prime minister in the last decade, right?
MINTON BEDDOES: I know. We change our prime ministers...

MINTON BEDDOES: ...You know, like we change our clothes nowadays. I - Prime Minister Burnham is a more natural politician than his predecessor. He's a man comfortable on social media. He's authentic, as they like to say. He's got some serious challenges. We don't have the world's reserve currency - the dollar. We're a much smaller market. And our debt - gilt yields. I mean, that's what British debt is called. Gilt yields are rising very sharply. And he has a big challenge.

You know, he needs to raise some money to make the books balance. That almost certainly has to come from cutting welfare spending, reforming - breaking some promises to pensioners. It's politically tough, but it has to be done. So one question is, will he be bold enough to do that, even though it was something that in their manifesto, his party said they wouldn't? Where would he find...
DAVIES: He's a Labour - (inaudible) - Labour Party, yup.

MINTON BEDDOES: He's a Labour prime minister, yes. The second is, will he do what is necessary to enable the British economy to grow faster? There's, again, a very well-known list of things that needs to be done - planning reform to make it easier to build houses, infrastructure reform, improvements in the tax system. You know, there are very kind of - the interesting thing about the U.K. is that there's a sort of - if you put a whole bunch of economists and technocrats in a room, they would come up with almost the same list of what needs to be done. It's just politically difficult.
DAVIES: What are his relationships like with President Trump and the EU, the European Union?

MINTON BEDDOES: Prime Minister Burnham met President Trump for the first time last week at the U.N. By all accounts, it was a cordial conversation. He's a very personable guy. He is very comfortable in his own skin. I think, even though he said some fairly, you know, critical things about President Trump in the past, he's a very affable man. I'm sure it would have been a good conversation. You know, Prime Minister Burnham, like every British prime minister right now, is having to navigate a path where you keep the U.S. on sight. I mean, we're very proud of the special relationship. We're very proud of, you know, having a kind of better relationship with the U.S. than many other Europeans, but at the same time, trying to work with other European countries.
DAVIES: OK, last question. At his speech in the United Nations, President Trump talked about U.S. power and I think said to the victor belongs the spoils. How was that received by Europeans?

MINTON BEDDOES: That goes back to what we were discussing earlier. I do think there's just a very different world view from this administration. It's one about, you know, exerting U.S. power. It's about power and power projection. And it's about victors and spoils. And that is very different from the alliance-based view that not just Europe, but America's other alliances, its Asian allies, have long thought the Western world was based on.

And I think everyone is coming to terms with that, is trying to understand whether this is President Trump specific or whether this is a new American posture, and what it means for others. It's trying to make sense of that. Every country I go to, every government official I talk to, wherever, that's the single most important question. Where is the U.S. going? What do they want? What kind of a world do they want? What role do they want to play? How do they see this working?

Because whether we all like it or not, the U.S. is the most important player in the room. And so we all have to understand what it wants. And for those of us who, you know, thought that a world based on rules and alliances was a world that was not just good for the world, but good for the U.S., this is a big change.
DAVIES: Right. And the question is whether there's a real change in the American mentality about it, or is it really just this particular president who is pretty unique?
MINTON BEDDOES: And I think we won't know the answer to that until after '28.
DAVIES: Right. Zanny Minton Beddoes, great to talk to you. Thank you so much for speaking with us.
MINTON BEDDOES: Thank you. Lovely to talk to you.
DAVIES: Zanny Minton Beddoes is editor in chief for The Economist. We recorded our conversation yesterday.

On tomorrow's show, Grammy-winning singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow. She just released her 12th studio album and is still touring. She says the job feels different now that she's in her 60s. I hope you can join us.

articles.title: Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
articles.author: Emily Feng

paras.en: Greetings from Syria, where time seems to melt as a glassmaker braves scorching temps
Our world as journalists can move fast; every day there's breaking news from all corners of the world, and we scramble to stay on top of multiple threads of information each day.

That is why I loved watching this glassmaker just outside the historic Old City in Damascus. In 100 degree summer heat, he patiently shaped cup after glass cup in the blistering furnace in front of him, seemingly impervious to the temperature.

Time seemed to matter less than the process of melting and stretching the hot, melted glass. He made cups and oil jars and decorative lamps in a variety of jewel colors, using techniques and styles that have not changed for decades. Watching his craft reminded me to slow down and enjoy the moment, too.

Even though his shop was right on the edge of the Old City of Damascus, it was largely empty. Syria's nearly 14-year civil war has ended, but the economy is still struggling, while inflation has ratcheted up the cost of living in the last year. Even a glass can be a luxury for some.

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss
articles.author: Imogen Foulkes

paras.en: Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss

BERN, Switzerland — Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice in 2026, marking another year of rapid decline. The loss reflects a wider global trend: Glaciers around the world have been shrinking at increasingly rapid rates, a phenomenon scientists link directly to global warming.

Matthias Huss leads Switzerland's glacier monitoring network, known as GLAMOS, which released the report alongside the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT). Each summer, Huss heads high into the mountains to measure the country's ice fields. For years, his research has documented rapid ice loss, with the decline peaking in 2022, when Switzerland recorded a record 6% loss in a single year.
At the end of this year's long, hot summer, Huss returned to some of the glaciers to find much of the ice gone.
"They are completely devoid of ice," he said. "It's a moon landscape that is dry and dead. There are some little remnants, some ice blocks still lying around and melting there on the hot rocks."

In other places, alpine plants are now seeding themselves in areas once covered by glaciers that were meters thick. This year's glacier monitoring report shows the ice loss in 2026 is 5.5%, and the only reason it is slightly lower than 2022's record is because there was slightly more winter snow covering the ice.
Ominously, though, Huss' research shows that individual glaciers, among them Switzerland's biggest, like the mighty Rhône and Aletsch, have suffered record ice loss this year.

Why is this important? Because these huge ice fields are often called Europe's water towers. They store winter snow and release it gently as it melts over the spring and summer. That snowmelt fills Europe's key waterways, like the Rhine and the Danube. The water is key to Europe's food supply, and much more.

"It's the food supply, it's the transportation chains," says Huss. This summer, as river levels sank, freight transport in the Rhine and Danube came to a standstill, and nuclear power stations, cooled by river water, had to be temporarily shut down.

This situation can only get worse if the melt continues. Although Europe's rivers did have some water this summer, it came not from seasonal snowmelt, but from the glaciers themselves melting. Once they are gone — and 1,200 smaller glaciers have disappeared in the last 50 years — drought could pose an existential threat to Europe's farmers.

There are other threats too. Glaciers and alpine permafrost are key to stability; they are a kind of glue that holds the mountains together. Without that glue, the risk of landslides and even flooding increases. Last year, the Swiss village of Blatten was wiped out when a fragile glacier crashed down, bringing the side of the mountain with it and destroying 300 homes.

Fortunately, the instability was being monitored, and Blatten's population was evacuated before the landslide. But one year later, they are still living in temporary accommodation, with no idea if they will ever be able to return to homes now buried under an estimated 9 million cubic meters of ice, rock and mud.
This summer, on Nepal's border with Tibet, the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods that killed at least 1,400 people.

Matthias Huss is cautious about making a direct link between climate change and such disasters. Mountain environments, he points out, have always been risky. "It's a bit more complicated than just saying it's warm and the glaciers are disappearing, so the mountains are falling apart and causing disasters like this," he explains.

But, he adds, climate change can be the catalyst for such natural disasters. "Combined with this heat, with the disappearance of the ice, with the warming of permafrost, climate change can be a triggering factor. That can just be the last bit that is missing to trigger such events."

And after years of monitoring the glaciers, Huss has little patience with those who still claim climate change does not exist. What is happening to the glaciers should be a warning sign, he argues. "Look at them, it's not a hoax. The evidence is clear, and it's been clear for decades. And I think many people have understood that it's time to act now."

Without action, Europe's beloved alpine landscape could, quite soon, look very different. If the planet keeps warming at its current rate, the glacier monitoring unit predicts, all the glaciers will be gone by the end of this century.

articles.title: Atlanta Dream advance to WNBA playoffs semifinals for first time since 2018 with Game 2 win

paras.en: The Atlanta Dream avoided a first-round playoff exit for the first time in four years.

Atlanta, which finished with the Eastern Conference’s best regular-season record, had little trouble dispatching the Washington Mystics in Game 2 of their first-round WNBA playoff series Tuesday night. Star guard Allisha Gray led the Dream with 22 points in the 83-75 victory, punching Atlanta’s ticket to the semifinals for the first time since 2018.

Atlanta’s postseason run will continue Sunday, when the Dream host Game 1 of the semifinals against New York. The Liberty made league history by sweeping Minnesota, becoming the first No. 8 seed to eliminate a No. 1 seed in the league's 30-year history.

Jordin Canada made 3-pointers on back-to-back possessions in the fourth quarter, and she added a jumper from the free-throw line on Atlanta’s next trip for an 89-70 lead with just under three minutes left on the clock.

Rhyne Howard, the top pick in the 2022 WNBA Draft, ended the night with 15 points before fouling out with just over six minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. Angel Reese also had 15 points and seven rebounds.
The Mystics committed 11 first-half turnovers.
Washington went on a 14-2 run starting in the third quarter to get within 65-62. But Atlanta scored the next 13 points, capped by a 3-pointer by Canada, to rebuild a double-digit lead at 78-62.

The Mystics were making their first playoff appearance since winning the 2019 WNBA championship, while the Dream have captured the conference title three times from 2010-13 but have never won a WNBA championship.
The Dallas Wings hosted the Golden State Valkyries in Wednesday's other first-round series matchup.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: White Sox, Yankees advance to next round with sweeps as Munetaka Murakami provides quote of the year

paras.en: Wednesday afternoon had plenty of potential for drama, with all four wild card series offering the potential for teams to advance into the division round of the Major League Baseball playoffs.

The first game of the quadruple-header, the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies, delivered in spades. A Bryce Harper misplay in the 7th inning allowed two Braves' runs to score, putting the Phillies on the brink of elimination. But Schwarber and Harper hit back-to-back homers in the 8th to tie it, and a 10th inning homer for Alec Bohm won it for Philadelphia to force a winner-take-all game three on Thursday.

Then there's the Houston Astros. The Astros entered game two needing a win to force a game three, sending their ace, Hunter Brown, to the mound against the White Sox' powerful lineup. 36 pitches, five hits, four runs, two errors and just two outs later, the White Sox had a 4-0 lead and Brown was out of the game.

That summed up Houston's series; just not quite good enough to overcome Chicago's offense. The White Sox, one of baseball's most strikeout-prone offenses, had 13 in Wednesday's game, but kept chipping away, fending off an attempted Astros comeback with a massive three-run homer from Chase Meidroth in the 6th inning to give them some breathing room.

Four combined innings from Jordan Hicks and Erick Fedde closed it out to send the White Sox through for a massive ALDS against their division rival Cleveland Guardians. But they weren't done with the entertainment quite yet.
In the postgame clubhouse celebrations, star first year third baseman Munetaka Murakami gave what might be the quote of the season. When asked how he felt, Murakami answered, "100."
A minute later, after being joined by another member of the White Sox staff, Murakami, covered in beer, added, "I'm drunk, I'm drunk. Yesterday, maybe hungover, you know?"
After the interviewer offered a gentle correction, he said, "No, not yesterday, tomorrow. Sorry, I don't speak English."

Meanwhile, on the other side of the American League postseason bracket, the New York Yankees had an opportunity to sweep the hated Boston Red Sox after a dominant 9-0 win in game one. And after Cam Schlittler's remarkable outing on Tuesday, Max Fried was nearly as good on Wednesday.

Six innings with just one run allowed, three hits, one walk and six strikeouts, enough for New York to take a 2-1 lead into the bottom of the sixth. Which is where everything imploded for Boston. Garrett Crochet, making his first appearance on a big league mound since late-April, took over, hoping to keep the Yankees at two.

Instead, Spencer Jones reached on a strikeout, then stole second and advanced to third on a throwing error from catcher Adley Rutschmann. George Lombard singled in a run, Jazz Chisholm poked one through the right side, Trent Grisham got a bunt down for a hit, knocking Crochet out of the game without getting an out. Garrett Whitlock came in to stop the bleeding, but after two more runs scored on a sac fly and groundout, Cody Bellinger delivered the big blow.
On a 1-0 changeup, Bellinger took advantage of the short right field porch and knocked in three to make it 8-1.
New York cruised home with a 9-2 win, setting up an ALDS matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.

There are a few big takeaways from these two sweeps, namely the importance of power in October baseball. It's an old adage that small ball wins against quality pitching, but it was the homers from Chicago in game one and two that gave them the edge, while Bellinger's bomb effectively put the game out of reach in the Bronx. Even without Aaron Judge, the Yankees' lineup outscored Boston 17-2. And with two days off before the start of the ALDS, Schlittler will be able to start in game two of the ALDS, with Gerrit Cole or Carlos Rodon available for game one.

While the Yankees are through, the other three teams left in the AL bracket are the Guardians, Rays and White Sox. Those teams rank 25th, 26th and 28th in total payroll respectively. There's a long ways to go to reach or win the World Series, but it's a bit of a tough look for MLB that the league office has spent the past few months preparing to lock players out by claiming that small market teams with low payrolls have no hope of meaningful baseball.
Pretty sure those three organizations should have hope. Saturday in Cleveland and Tampa should be a blast. Playoff baseball always is.

articles.title: Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescues man stranded atop overturned truck in rapidly rising floodwaters

paras.en: Dramatic video shows an Arizona sheriff's helicopter crew rescuing a man stranded on top of his overturned truck as rapidly moving floodwaters surrounded the vehicle.

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said its Fox 1 aviation crew responded Tuesday morning to a flooded wash in Tonopah, where deputies found the man sitting atop the overturned vehicle with water rushing around him.
Video released by authorities shows the man perched on the truck as muddy floodwaters rush past him.
Because of the dangerous conditions, first responders determined that directly reaching the man was too risky and decided a "hoist rescue" would be the safest option.
The video shows a Fox 1 crew member being lowered to the vehicle to secure the man in a rescue harness before both are hoisted to safety.
The man was taken to the riverbank, where fire personnel were waiting, according to the sheriff's office.
The helicopter's pilot, Rich Dickner, told CBS News that the water was quickly rising around the vehicle.
"We didn't waste much time," Dickner said.
"As opposed to when we first got there, you can see the water line on the video — it's below the window — and it had risen up to the top of the window," he continued. "So there was that urgency."
People Magazine reported that Deputy Lindsey Smith was lowered approximately 80 feet from the helicopter toward the overturned truck.
She initially struggled to get her footing before securing herself to the vehicle, according to the report.
The entire rescue took less than five minutes, authorities said.
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office credited the crew's swift response with getting the man to safety.
"Thanks to the skill and quick response of our Aviation crew, the subject was safely brought to shore," the sheriff's office said.
The Weather Channel reported that remnants of Hurricane Polo brought historic rainfall to parts of the Desert Southwest, contributing to dangerous flash flooding.
The Flood Control District of Maricopa County warned drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roads.
"Remember: Conditions can change fast. If you encounter a flooded roadway, Turn Around, Don't Drown."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for additional information.

articles.title: Australian couple among passengers on diverted flydubai flight to Israel, embassy says
articles.author: Tess Ikonomou

paras.en: Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack, according to the Israeli embassy.
The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided.
The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes.

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.
“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”
Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued following the attack.
“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.
